nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Crevalle Jack
Scientific Name:  Caranx hippos

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Carangidae

Other Common Names: Jack (312 664 834), common jack (264 265 327), crevalle (312 327 834); runner, �Jenny Lind,� rudder fish (312); yellowtail jack, hardtail jack, amber jack (582 664); cavally, horse crevalle, horse mackerel (834).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Meat is generally considered to be �medium� quality and is therefore not particularly sought after by commercial fishermen (312).  Commercial catch is concentrated in western Florida; commonly found in markets in other portions of its range (47 312 364 791 834).  Generally marketed fresh (791).  Florida landings in 1989 amounted to 1,668,816 lbs. worth $259,769, with most fish landed at west coast ports (902).  In the Indian river Lagoon (IRL) jack crevalle are often sold as crab bait(997).

Recreational: Regarded as a nuisance by many anglers since these fish take considerable time to land on light tackle due to their hard fighting ability (327 702 932), but other fishermen enjoy this challenging fish (47).  Generally regarded as only poor to good as a food fish (312 327 791 834 871 932), the flesh can be very good when properly prepared and cooked (364).

Ecological Role: A large carnivore highly predatory on other fish (69 312 550 696).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Uruguay, primarily in shallow continental waters; rare in the Bahamas and only a few reported from the West Indies where it is probably uncommon (49 327 363 312 791 871 932).  Relatively more common in northern part of range (932).  Once thought to be circumtropical, it is now known to be restricted to the western Atlantic with geminate species found in the eastern Atlantic and eastern Pacific (791 1037).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (265 788 789 791 891 1030).  Reported as abundant in several Florida estuaries (515 702 789) and as the most common carangid species at Cedar Key (581) and Tampa Bay (664) and the IRL (993 997).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
A large pelagic fish common in offshore waters.  Most active during the day in the upper water column.  Both adults and juveniles are schooling, but some large adults are solitary (19 47 116 550 664 694 696 791).

Mobility and Migration: Little is known, probably a complicated pattern of spawning and developmental migrations, and temperature induced movements.  A concentrated spawning migration is improbable due to the long length of the spawning season (481).  Juveniles (90 to 285 mm TL) enter bays and estuaries from the Gulf when the water temperature is above 20.0 C (47 255).  Probably migrate south or move into warmer, offshore waters during colder months (49).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: Pelagic, probably an offshore existence that may be associated with offshore currents.  Taken in euhaline waters (47 49).

Juveniles: Probably migrates inshore during early juvenile stage and selectively inhabits inshore waters during late juvenile stage.  Has been found in bays, Gulf passes, sounds, estuaries, brackish lakes and ponds, canals, and rivers (312 255 651 790 163 19 664 702 264 322 374 39 694 157 116 696 47).  Found in salinities ranging from fresh to hypersaline waters (31 47 116 157 224 255 264 515 550 548 582 651 694 696 790 848 871) and a depth range of 0.3 to 27.5 m (322 651 786).

Adults: Pelagic, associated with waters of continental shelf and continental islands (49).  Collections have also been made in inshore and even brackish waters, upstream in coastal rivers, and commonly on shallow flats (363 790 791).  Larger adults remain offshore and are seldom taken in bays and other inshore waters (47 116 255 791).  Reported to occur from fresh to hypersaline waters (515 603 790 791).  Found in a wide range of depths from shallow mud flats to offshore waters over continental shelf (47 791).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: Because this is a pelagic schooling fish, it has not been identified with a particular bottom type, but it has been recorded from bottoms of mud, sand, and hard packed bottoms with a mud and algae film (47 264 582).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Larvae: Reported from temperatures ranging from 20.4 - 29.4 C (363).

Juveniles/adults: Collected over a temperature range of 15.0 - 38.0 C (116 224 264 265 312 372 548 550 574 603 702 709 800 887 936).  Apparent preferred temperature range reported as 25.0 - 29.9 C (550).  Lower lethal limit for juveniles is around 7.4 - 10.0 C (236 329).  Reported as one of the species killed by freezes in the IRL (236 997) and at Sanibel Island, FL (1068), and is listed as one of the species that is �always hurt� by these freezes (836).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Larvae: 35.2 - 36.7 ppt (49).

Juvenile/adult: Euryhaline, found in waters of 0.0 - 60.0 ppt salinity (254 255 582 261 651 264 265 188 224 603 550 694 157 116 548 696 372 709 31).  In the northern Gulf of Mexico, fish 30 - 285 mm TL were mostly caught in salinities above 30.0 ppt (255), and the majority of fish 20 to 180 mm TL (average size of 60 mm TL) were collected at 10.0 - 19.9 ppt (550).  Florida collections include individuals taken in freshwater (264 515 790 848), and at salinities of 24.8 - 35.5 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River (265), 6.0 - 48.0 ppt in Everglades National Park (603 702), 35.6 - 37.8 ppt at Matecumbe Key, and 1.5 - 36.6 ppt in Jupiter inlet (887).

nodes.title: Oxygen
nodes.body: Juveniles collected in waters with a D.O. range of 4.0 - 7.5 ppm (31).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, sexes separate. External fertilization, broadcast spawner.

Spawning Strategy:  Apparently occurs offshore primarily south of the Florida Straits (47 49 206 322).  Season is thought to be March to September (49).  Sabins (1066) caught his smallest individuals (22 - 40 mm) during June and August in Louisiana.  In Texas, Hoese (322) also collected his smallest specimens from June through August.  Ditty et al (802), summarizing the literature, reported the presence of larvae identified as C. hipposlatus from March through August in the Gulf of Mexico.

Fecundity: Unknown. The ovaries of a 520 mm TL female with well developed eggs were 110 by 60 mm (40).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg/larvae: no information

Juvenile: The minimum size for this stage is 8.0 mm SL.  From 12.7 - 22.1 mm SL, 3 - 6 spines present on lower limb of preopercle; actual size at loss of preopercular spines varies somewhat and may be associated with movement to inshore waters (49).  At 15.3 mm SL, 3 vertical stripes on body, fourth and fifth bars present as undivided pigment mass.  At 25 mm SL, a small patch of scales apparent on chest just in front of pelvics; by 80.5 mm SL, a patch of scales present along each cleithrum and laterally along insertion of each pelvic fin.  At 16.1 mm SL, a few scutes completely developed; by 100 mm nearly all scutes completely developed.  Age and size at sexual maturity uncertain.  Males with developed testes range from 540 to 690 mm SL (49) and a 406 mm SL female was reported as having well developed eggs (40).  Juveniles enter trawl catches in June and December in the IRL (997).

Adult: Females are probably larger than males on the average.  The largest recorded fish is 980 mm SL, but sizes up to 1500 mm SL may be possible (49 788).  Reaches to 9 kg (788).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: A voracious carnivore, predatory on small schooling fishes of the coastal zone (312 616).  Has been observed in Florida feeding wildly along shorelines on larval fishes, primarily lady fish, anchovies, and cyprinodonts (702).  Small jacks were found to prey mostly on a variety of clupeids, while medium size fish usually ate clupeids and sparids, and large fish consumed various clupeids, caragids, and sparids (616).  Large fish appear to be more opportunistic than smaller ones, but food availability seems to be a major factor as the diet changes between sizes, seasons, areas, and years.  Brevoortia patronus is a favorite food (69 696) but also feeds on Harengula jaguana, Anchoa sp., Sardinella aurita, Chloroscombrus chrysurus, Lagodon rhomboides, Hemiramphus sp., Caranx hippos, Trichiurus lepturus, and C. chrysurus.  Penaeid shrimp and portunid crabs form the second most important prey item depending on area.  In addition numerous other fish are consumed as well as squid, bivalves, gastropods, echinoderms, sea grasses, algae, sand, and wood (47 163 515 616).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predators include Sphyraena barracuda and Thunnus atlanticus (49).

Parasites/Diseases:  observed on this species are: Nematodes - Ascaris sp.; Cestodes - Tetrarhyncus bisculatus; Trematodes - Distomum appendiculatum, D. tenue, Gasterostomum arcuatum, and G. gracilescens (413).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title:  Crevalle jack (Caranx hippos)

FLELMR CODE: 1625

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
7/08/93. T.D. Philipps; Mote Marine Laboratory
4/04/94. S. Traxler; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Crevalle Jack
Scientific Name:  Caranx hippos

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Carangidae

Other Common Names: Jack (312 664 834), common jack (264 265 327), crevalle (312 327 834); runner, �Jenny Lind,� rudder fish (312); yellowtail jack, hardtail jack, amber jack (582 664); cavally, horse crevalle, horse mackerel (834).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial: Meat is generally considered to be �medium� quality and is therefore not particularly sought after by commercial fishermen (312).  Commercial catch is concentrated in western Florida; commonly found in markets in other portions of its range (47 312 364 791 834).  Generally marketed fresh (791).  Florida landings in 1989 amounted to 1,668,816 lbs. worth $259,769, with most fish landed at west coast ports (902).  In the Indian river Lagoon (IRL) jack crevalle are often sold as crab bait(997).

Recreational: Regarded as a nuisance by many anglers since these fish take considerable time to land on light tackle due to their hard fighting ability (327 702 932), but other fishermen enjoy this challenging fish (47).  Generally regarded as only poor to good as a food fish (312 327 791 834 871 932), the flesh can be very good when properly prepared and cooked (364).

Ecological Role: A large carnivore highly predatory on other fish (69 312 550 696).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to Uruguay, primarily in shallow continental waters; rare in the Bahamas and only a few reported from the West Indies where it is probably uncommon (49 327 363 312 791 871 932).  Relatively more common in northern part of range (932).  Once thought to be circumtropical, it is now known to be restricted to the western Atlantic with geminate species found in the eastern Atlantic and eastern Pacific (791 1037).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (265 788 789 791 891 1030).  Reported as abundant in several Florida estuaries (515 702 789) and as the most common carangid species at Cedar Key (581) and Tampa Bay (664) and the IRL (993 997).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
A large pelagic fish common in offshore waters.  Most active during the day in the upper water column.  Both adults and juveniles are schooling, but some large adults are solitary (19 47 116 550 664 694 696 791).

Mobility and Migration: Little is known, probably a complicated pattern of spawning and developmental migrations, and temperature induced movements.  A concentrated spawning migration is improbable due to the long length of the spawning season (481).  Juveniles (90 to 285 mm TL) enter bays and estuaries from the Gulf when the water temperature is above 20.0 C (47 255).  Probably migrate south or move into warmer, offshore waters during colder months (49).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Eggs/larvae: Pelagic, probably an offshore existence that may be associated with offshore currents.  Taken in euhaline waters (47 49).

Juveniles: Probably migrates inshore during early juvenile stage and selectively inhabits inshore waters during late juvenile stage.  Has been found in bays, Gulf passes, sounds, estuaries, brackish lakes and ponds, canals, and rivers (312 255 651 790 163 19 664 702 264 322 374 39 694 157 116 696 47).  Found in salinities ranging from fresh to hypersaline waters (31 47 116 157 224 255 264 515 550 548 582 651 694 696 790 848 871) and a depth range of 0.3 to 27.5 m (322 651 786).

Adults: Pelagic, associated with waters of continental shelf and continental islands (49).  Collections have also been made in inshore and even brackish waters, upstream in coastal rivers, and commonly on shallow flats (363 790 791).  Larger adults remain offshore and are seldom taken in bays and other inshore waters (47 116 255 791).  Reported to occur from fresh to hypersaline waters (515 603 790 791).  Found in a wide range of depths from shallow mud flats to offshore waters over continental shelf (47 791).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content: Because this is a pelagic schooling fish, it has not been identified with a particular bottom type, but it has been recorded from bottoms of mud, sand, and hard packed bottoms with a mud and algae film (47 264 582).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Larvae: Reported from temperatures ranging from 20.4 - 29.4 C (363).

Juveniles/adults: Collected over a temperature range of 15.0 - 38.0 C (116 224 264 265 312 372 548 550 574 603 702 709 800 887 936).  Apparent preferred temperature range reported as 25.0 - 29.9 C (550).  Lower lethal limit for juveniles is around 7.4 - 10.0 C (236 329).  Reported as one of the species killed by freezes in the IRL (236 997) and at Sanibel Island, FL (1068), and is listed as one of the species that is �always hurt� by these freezes (836).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Larvae: 35.2 - 36.7 ppt (49).

Juvenile/adult: Euryhaline, found in waters of 0.0 - 60.0 ppt salinity (254 255 582 261 651 264 265 188 224 603 550 694 157 116 548 696 372 709 31).  In the northern Gulf of Mexico, fish 30 - 285 mm TL were mostly caught in salinities above 30.0 ppt (255), and the majority of fish 20 to 180 mm TL (average size of 60 mm TL) were collected at 10.0 - 19.9 ppt (550).  Florida collections include individuals taken in freshwater (264 515 790 848), and at salinities of 24.8 - 35.5 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River (265), 6.0 - 48.0 ppt in Everglades National Park (603 702), 35.6 - 37.8 ppt at Matecumbe Key, and 1.5 - 36.6 ppt in Jupiter inlet (887).

sections.heading: Oxygen
sections.content: Juveniles collected in waters with a D.O. range of 4.0 - 7.5 ppm (31).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, sexes separate. External fertilization, broadcast spawner.

Spawning Strategy:  Apparently occurs offshore primarily south of the Florida Straits (47 49 206 322).  Season is thought to be March to September (49).  Sabins (1066) caught his smallest individuals (22 - 40 mm) during June and August in Louisiana.  In Texas, Hoese (322) also collected his smallest specimens from June through August.  Ditty et al (802), summarizing the literature, reported the presence of larvae identified as C. hipposlatus from March through August in the Gulf of Mexico.

Fecundity: Unknown. The ovaries of a 520 mm TL female with well developed eggs were 110 by 60 mm (40).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg/larvae: no information

Juvenile: The minimum size for this stage is 8.0 mm SL.  From 12.7 - 22.1 mm SL, 3 - 6 spines present on lower limb of preopercle; actual size at loss of preopercular spines varies somewhat and may be associated with movement to inshore waters (49).  At 15.3 mm SL, 3 vertical stripes on body, fourth and fifth bars present as undivided pigment mass.  At 25 mm SL, a small patch of scales apparent on chest just in front of pelvics; by 80.5 mm SL, a patch of scales present along each cleithrum and laterally along insertion of each pelvic fin.  At 16.1 mm SL, a few scutes completely developed; by 100 mm nearly all scutes completely developed.  Age and size at sexual maturity uncertain.  Males with developed testes range from 540 to 690 mm SL (49) and a 406 mm SL female was reported as having well developed eggs (40).  Juveniles enter trawl catches in June and December in the IRL (997).

Adult: Females are probably larger than males on the average.  The largest recorded fish is 980 mm SL, but sizes up to 1500 mm SL may be possible (49 788).  Reaches to 9 kg (788).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: A voracious carnivore, predatory on small schooling fishes of the coastal zone (312 616).  Has been observed in Florida feeding wildly along shorelines on larval fishes, primarily lady fish, anchovies, and cyprinodonts (702).  Small jacks were found to prey mostly on a variety of clupeids, while medium size fish usually ate clupeids and sparids, and large fish consumed various clupeids, caragids, and sparids (616).  Large fish appear to be more opportunistic than smaller ones, but food availability seems to be a major factor as the diet changes between sizes, seasons, areas, and years.  Brevoortia patronus is a favorite food (69 696) but also feeds on Harengula jaguana, Anchoa sp., Sardinella aurita, Chloroscombrus chrysurus, Lagodon rhomboides, Hemiramphus sp., Caranx hippos, Trichiurus lepturus, and C. chrysurus.  Penaeid shrimp and portunid crabs form the second most important prey item depending on area.  In addition numerous other fish are consumed as well as squid, bivalves, gastropods, echinoderms, sea grasses, algae, sand, and wood (47 163 515 616).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predators include Sphyraena barracuda and Thunnus atlanticus (49).

Parasites/Diseases:  observed on this species are: Nematodes - Ascaris sp.; Cestodes - Tetrarhyncus bisculatus; Trematodes - Distomum appendiculatum, D. tenue, Gasterostomum arcuatum, and G. gracilescens (413).
